Ellul's notion of the autonomization of technique helps explain how efficiency comes to operate as the dominant criterion of social organization. Technique no longer figures as a mere instrument subordinate to external ends and becomes a system of rationalization capable of conditioning practices, expectations and institutions. In this shift, even Law comes under pressure from criteria of performance, operability and functional adaptation.

This key appears, on a smaller scale, in the way platform-operated games normalize continuous updates, recalibrations and reconfigurations of value. The unilateral alteration of a cosmetic item or the redesign of a character does not arise as an extraordinary event, but as an ordinary manifestation of a system that adjusts itself according to internal criteria of efficiency, balance and retention. Ellul is drawn on<1><2>43</2></1> to explain why this logic tends to shift the debate from the realm of ends, that is, what must be preserved and the expectations that were created, to the realm of method, that is, what “works best” for the system. Technical design thus reveals itself as a locus of power and as a relevant dimension for the subsequent legal qualification.

In Ellul, the conversion of technique into environment stems from the modern shift of technique from a set of instruments to a totalizing rationality, present in methods of organization, procedures, decision-making patterns and ways of administering reality. Unified by measurable efficiency, technique comes to operate less as a means subordinate to substantive ends and more as a regime capable of reorganizing values, expectations and institutions, reconfiguring the very grammar of what counts as “adequate”, “better” and “possible” in everyday life. For this reason, the technical phenomenon cannot be reduced to machines or material <1>p. 93</1> apparatuses, since it includes organizational factors and utilitarian modes of thought that structure the social <2>Ellul</2><3>(Ellul, 1968, p. 1-5)</3>.

In developing the characterology of technique<1><2>44</2></1>, Ellul describes an evolution marked by the pursuit of efficiency, the expansion of automatism and the formation of self-augmenting structures, traits that distinguish modern technique from earlier forms. In this picture, technique presents itself as indifferent to moral judgment and breaks with the belief that technical progress would, in itself, amount to human progress <3>Ellul</3><4>(Ellul, 1968, p. 117)</4>. The distinction between ancient and modern technique makes this shift explicit: while the former remains tied to empiricism and to slow development, the latter is characterized by universality, objective rationality, artificiality, automatism, self-augmentation, indivisibility and autonomy, with effects that can reach every aspect of human life, including the reduction of man to the condition of an object <5>Ellul</5><6>(Ellul, 1968, p. 66-80)</6>.

The rationality of modern technique operates by applying logic to the pursuit of maximum efficiency, which tends to demote values that cannot be translated into measurable performance. In this context Ellul describes the automatism of technical choice as a blind search for the “best way” to perform a task, with the loss of a holistic criterion of adequacy and a growing indifference to the social, moral or aesthetic consequences produced by the method <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 82-88)</2>. Once this automatism sets in, the question of what must be preserved gives way to the question of what best keeps the system running.

In the <1>League of Legends</1> ecosystem, the match management algorithm makes this autonomy especially visible, because matchmaking presents itself as an optimization problem, and not as a deliberation on the best possible experience for each individual. The company describes the need to simultaneously balance “fair matches”, “position preference” and “fast queues”, admitting that, under real constraints, the system shifts weight among these criteria and relaxes parameters so that the match can take place <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2026a)</3>. In this grammar, “fairness” no longer operates as moral language and instead functions as a statistical target, tied to an approximate 50% probability of victory for each team, produced by averaging MMR<4><5>45</5></4> <6>Riot Games</6><7>(Riot Games, 2026a)</7>. Ludic enjoyment does not disappear, but it is compressed <8>p. 94</8> by a method that must operate under scarcity of supply, schedules, an unequal distribution of roles and variations in skill, turning the player into a performance variable in a self-adjusting architecture.

This point is reinforced when the company itself explains that MMR is a hidden number, designed to operate in <1>back-end</1><2><3>46</3></2><4> </4>systems and to guide how each person is placed in balanced matches, while the visible rank works as a pedagogical and progressive translation of that measure<5><6>47</6></5> <7>Riot Games</7><8>(Riot Games, 2026c)</8>. Here, technical autonomy lies in the shift of the relevant decision-making procedure to a non-transparent layer, which defines what counts as balance and continuously adjusts matchmaking criteria to preserve the stability of the ecosystem. When queue time becomes the decisive constraint, matchmaking rules tend to loosen, and the system begins to seek the “next best” instead of the “ideal”, because the method requires that the match take place within an acceptable time horizon<9><10>48</10></9> <11>League of Legends Wiki</11><12>(League of Legends Wiki, [202-?]i)</12><13><14>49</14></13>. The result matches the effect Ellul describes: a technical choice presented as inevitable because it “works best” for the system, shifting the debate from ends to the continuous adjustment of method.

This normalization of technical mutability also appears in the contractual frame by which the service authorizes itself to evolve continuously. In the Terms of Service, the user agrees that Riot may change, modify, update, suspend, “nerf” or restrict access to features and parts of the service, including through automatic background updates, with or without prior notice<1><2>50</2></1> <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>. The vocabulary that legitimizes this plasticity is that of constant <5>p. 95</5> improvement, evolution and security, and the user's experience comes to be treated as an adjustable dimension of systemic functioning. In an Ellulian key, technique ceases to appear as a means subordinate to the end of entertainment and asserts itself as a self-justified environment, capable of absorbing enjoyment as a management variable to preserve the stability of the ecosystem.

As regards artificiality, Ellul asserts that modern technique stands opposed to nature and constitutes a system made up of artificial means, in which technical intervention reduces the real to a “logical scheme” and reorganizes facts and phenomena according to internal demands of rationalization <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 82)</2>. This environment breaks with traditional grounding, since technique rejects tradition and comes to rely on the combination and accelerated evolution of earlier technical processes, at a pace too fast for full integration into the accumulated cultural fabric <3>Ellul</3><4>(Ellul, 1968, p. 13)</4>.

The economy, in this picture, becomes progressively dependent on technique and its methods, to the point at which technique ceases to function as a subordinate economic instrument and comes to dictate the conditions of the economic game itself <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 152-162)</2>. Along these lines, the economy becomes intimately dependent on technique, seeking to adapt to its demands and using its methods to achieve objectives.

The relationship between technique and the State reinforces this institutional diagnosis. Ellul characterizes technique as a fundamental instrument of state power, especially in the modern State, increasingly dependent on technical procedures to administer, regulate, control and wage war <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 233-238)</2>. This dependence shapes the state structure, favors centralization and bureaucratization and alters the very nature of the State, which comes to operate as a technical organism, limited by the forms of perception and decision that its administrative rationality makes available <3>Ellul</3><4>(Ellul, 1968, p. 257-260)</4>.

In examining techniques directly aimed at man, oriented toward modifying behavior, needs and subjective dispositions, Ellul identifies psychological, sociological and biometric techniques as expressive manifestations of attempts to control and manipulate the human person <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 325-331)</2>. The author also observes that the technical modification of space itself can condition behavior, which extends the problem beyond isolated instruments and reaches the environmental organization of human action <3>Ellul</3><4>(Ellul, 1968, p. 331-335)</4>. This reflection directly concerns digital ecosystems, <5>p. 96</5> in which environments of interface, reward, punishment and visibility are designed to guide conduct, modulate expectations and reduce practical margins of freedom.

The Ellulian reference to “inevitability” must be taken as a critical description of a system effect<1><2>51</2></1>, that is, of the tendency toward naturalization and self-justification of the technical, and not as a normative thesis according to which history would be closed to contestation. What matters, above all, is the mechanism by which technique presents itself as destiny and removes from public visibility the choices and costs embedded in its procedures. This hermeneutic caution preserves Ellul's diagnostic force without converting critique into fatalism, making it possible to place back into the design of infrastructures the disputes, alternatives and ends that the language of efficiency tends to obscure.

At the end of his work, Ellul questions the belief that technical progress is an objective synonym of human progress and appeals to individual and collective responsibility in the face of technique <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 441-445)</2>. In his view, society must seek effective forms of control over technical development in order to orient it toward the human good, even as he recognizes that man cannot fully adapt to the technical phenomenon.

This set makes it possible to identify the point of passage to the legal problem: by reducing the real to a “logical scheme” and refusing external judgments when the problem is presented as technical, technique compresses the space for deliberation on ends and shifts the decision to the language of efficiency <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 82; p. 136)</2>. What cannot be rationalized tends to be treated as irrelevant, impracticable or external to the functioning of the system. Hence the importance of placing technical choices back in the field of attribution, since the appearance of neutrality may conceal ends, costs and distributions of risk that directly affect the consumption experience.

With this, technique comes to organize the very perception of the social world. When the economy, public administration and entertainment operate under this rationality, the individual is recoded into indicators of performance, available time, engagement and risk. <1>p. 97</1> Technique ceases to be an accessory of social life and comes to define what can be seen, measured, governed and contested.

This reorganization also becomes institutionally entrenched. At the level of operative rationality, the shift appears when, to escape “arbitrariness and subjectivity” and “ethical judgment”, technique demands that reality be reduced to number <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 17)</2>. Law is affected by this pressure not only because it comes to deal with technically complex objects, but because its own practice can be absorbed by criteria of efficiency. For the “technician of law”, the decisive reference tends to shift from the normative end to the efficiency of application, since “all law depends on its efficiency” and “a law that is not applied is not a law” <3>Ellul</3><4>(Ellul, 1968, p. 299)</4>. Under this pressure for performance and operability, normative conflicts tend to be recast as problems of management and compliance, which makes it harder to deliberate on ends when technical autonomy narrows the room for choice over collective means and directions <5>Ellul</5><6>(Ellul, 1968, p. 143)</6>.

Transposed to digital consumption, this diagnosis makes it possible to interpret electronic games, streaming platforms and social networks not as isolated applications, but as specific manifestations of this technique-environment. Interfaces, algorithms, reward systems and mechanisms of artificial scarcity are organized under criteria of efficiency, retention and continuous governance. What is prepared here under the category of Immaterial Object of Consumption emerges precisely from this operation: it is an object of functional and continued existence, inseparable from the technical infrastructure that gives it access, utility, stability and practical meaning.

For this reason, a strictly material reading of consumption does not adequately capture the phenomenon. When the object is inseparable from the technical architecture<1><2>52</2></1> that sustains it, the central problem ceases to be only the existence of a quality defect in an isolated product and comes to include the way technique organizes possibilities of use, permanence, loss or degradation over time.

Ellul is not called upon to sustain a generic critique of technological modernity, but to make intelligible the technical order in which the IOC is formed. In digital ecosystems, the consumer relationship is not reduced to the exchange of a performance for a price; it is installed in an environment organized by metrics, automatisms, access regimes and procedures of <1>p. 98</1> continuous updating. The enjoyment of the object becomes inseparable from the functioning of the technical ambience, which is why architecture and governance cannot be treated as externalities of supply, but as material dimensions of the consumer relationship itself. Next, this ambience will be combined with the media reconfiguration of experience, with Postman, and with cultural and advertising desymbolization, with Vanderburg, preparing the passage to the Lex Plataformae and to semiotic vulnerability.

Titled <1>A Técnica e o Desafio do Sécul</1>o, the paradigmatic work at the center of the thought of the French historian, sociologist and jurist Jacques Ellul, originally published in 1954, offers an important conceptual overview of technique, its development and its influence on contemporary society. The discussion is divided into six parts, each exploring different facets of the technical phenomenon. What matters here is to highlight a few elements that help explain how modern technique becomes a structuring environment of social life and, consequently, of the forms of digital consumption. <2>↩</2>

Postman<1><2>53</2></1> (2006) makes it possible to understand media as a form of organization of social knowledge, and not merely as a channel for the circulation of messages. The passage from electronic to digital media deepens this shift: public space is progressively recoded by the grammar of spectacle, while the ways of producing, legitimizing and recognizing knowledge come to depend on formats, rhythms and criteria of attention specific to the dominant media ecology. This diagnosis has a direct impact on the way consumers perceive products, services and platforms.

In media ecologies, the decisive problem lies not only in the content that circulates, but in the form of circulation that comes to organize perception and credibility. Formats, rhythms, expectations of attention and criteria of relevance become embodied social habits. At this point, Postman's reading serves to describe the passage from a culture strongly organized by argumentative linearity to one traversed by the performativity of show business, in which visibility, impact and retention come to condition the way something becomes socially intelligible.

Postman's contribution matters not as nostalgia for print culture, but as a key for understanding that each medium establishes its own ecology of perception and knowledge. By recoding politics, religion and education in terms of entertainment, television alters criteria of informational relevance, credibility and acceptability of public debate. In the digital environment, this shift does not disappear: it is radicalized by <1>p. 99</1> platforms capable of personalizing flows, modulating visibility and transforming attention into an operational variable.

For consumption, this shift is decisive. When relevance, credibility and acceptability come to be modulated by entertainment formats, the perception of value is also reorganized. The consumption decision no longer depends primarily on checks of adequacy and performance and is instead mediated by regimes of attention, reputation and belonging. Within them, the form of presentation and the dramaturgy of the offer, expressed in storefronts, <1>trailers</1>, events and narratives of permanent updating, becomes a constitutive component of the experience consumed.

In the platform-operated game, this reconfiguration appears in concentrated form. The value of the object is not apprehended only through its functional characteristics, but through the public staging that precedes and accompanies it. Official media transform items, characters, seasons and events into shareable narrative repertoires, converting purchase and enjoyment into symbolic continuity within the ecosystem.

Riot Games' audiovisual production functions, in this sense, as a device of knowledge applied to consumption. Media do not limit themselves to publicizing what already exists, since they are capable of defining what counts as relevant information about the object, which traits should be perceived as essential and which affects can operate as criteria of evaluation. The consumer does not need to know the item as a technical structure to recognize it as a desirable good. They know it as image, narrative and repertoire of socially shareable signals, produced and distributed by official channels in the format of spectacle. A music video such as <1>POP/STARS</1> <2>fonte</2><3>(K/DA..., 2018)</3>, an example of the productivity of the <4>Riot </4> <5>Music</5> division, is especially relevant because it transforms a set of cosmetics into a public cultural reference prior to use, operating as a matrix of intelligibility for the purchase and for the social recognition of the item's value.

The same logic intensifies in the seasonal <1>cinematics</1>, through which the company presents a visual synthesis of the universe and of the expectations it wishes to stabilize as a common horizon. <2>Still Here</2> <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024d)</4>, in presenting itself as a season-opening cinematic and condensing the editorial statement “<5>Fight for tomorrow</5>”<6><7>54</7></6>, makes explicit this function of guiding <8>p. 100</8> the gaze and expectation. Here, the epistemology of consumption does not correspond to expanded access to data about the object, but to a form of mediated knowledge in which the image becomes a criterion of pragmatic truth. The item is what the media allow it to be seen as being. Consequently, utility ceases to be the sole axis of decision and gives way to aesthetic intelligibility, to narrative promise and to the repertoire of signs that enables belonging and distinction within the community.

This media reconfiguration finds a correspondence in the declared norm of the ecosystem itself, insofar as the contract describes skins and related items as licensed Virtual Content, linked to the account, and not as the consumer's property<1><2>55</2></1>. When the offer is structured as spectacle, but the object is legally presented as revocable or modifiable access, a tension central to the thesis is formed: the consumer knows the good through its aesthetic and community staging, while its stability remains subject to the platform's technical-contractual regime. For this reason, changes to visuals, animation, effects, symbolic balancing or access conditions cannot be treated merely as functional corrections, bugs or graphic improvements<3><4>56</4></3>. In this picture, the epistemology of consumption becomes inseparable from the media architecture that frames what the object “is” and from the contractual regime that controls how much of this “being” remains stable.

The consumption promise is, therefore, publicly performed, while enjoyment is mediated by signals of visibility, prestige and belonging. The unilateral alteration of the item or the character may affect not only a technical utility, but the symbolic position that was produced by the platform itself. Postman contributes precisely at this point, since his critique, formerly directed at <1>show business</1>, once updated by metrified digital ecosystems <2>p. 101</2>, makes it possible to understand how criteria of credibility and value are reorganized until the design of the offer and the dramaturgy of permanence become part of the content consumed.

According to Postman, the rise of television to hegemony among the media redefined the parameters by which information is processed, truths are conceived and intellectual capacities are evaluated. The passage from typographic culture to television altered not only the medium of communication; it transformed criteria of truth, intelligence and seriousness in public discourse <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 23])</2>. Under this regime, television favors fragmentation, reduces the possibility of more complex discourse and replaces the argumentative coherence of typographic culture with public conversations marked by triviality, broken sequence and the progressive abandonment of logic, reason and the rules of contradiction <3>Postman</3><4>(Postman, 2006, [p. 58])</4>.

Politics is one of the central manifestations<1><2>57</2></1> of this shift. For Postman, television reconfigures it as a branch of show business, transforming public debate into a product compatible with entertainment <3>Postman</3><4>(Postman, 2006, [p. 16])</4>. Campaigns come to operate through the formation of images, the management of performances and the replacement of ideologies by appearance, as if political value could be absorbed by the efficacy of ready-made scenes. In this context, “knowing” politics comes to mean visual familiarity, and not necessarily understanding structured by language and discourse <5>Postman</5><6>(Postman, 2006, [p. 86])</6>.

In education, the pursuit of entertainment also alters the criteria of learning. The critical and in-depth process loses ground to recreational forms of access to content, while difficulty, intellectual discipline and the duration of cognitive effort come to be seen as obstacles to efficient communication <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 146])</2>. Hence the assertion that television and image culture do not constitute merely a style of communication, but a threat to the foundations of liberal democracy, insofar as they strike at its material basis: freedom of information <3>Postman</3><4>(Postman, 2006, [p. 91])</4>.

The conversion of the public space into show business matters less for its sectoral object than for its mechanism. The point lies in the formation of a regime in which signs and performances progressively replace arguments as criteria of recognition, <1>p. 102</1> trust and value. This structure is decisive for the thesis because, on digital platforms, the object of consumption is not merely presented to the consumer; it is staged in formats that produce trust, urgency and adherence, making the consumption experience inseparable from the ecology of attention in which it is promoted and enjoyed.

The central mechanism is fragmentation. The image dismembers reality by tearing moments from their contexts and juxtaposing events without logical or historical connection, recreating the world as a series of idiosyncratic happenings <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 55])</2>. In this environment, intelligence comes to mean knowing many things, and not knowing about them, that is, accumulating disconnected data without in-depth understanding <3>Postman</3><4>(Postman, 2006, [p. 74])</4>. Disinformation, therefore, is not limited to falsity, since it also manifests itself as displaced, irrelevant, fragmented or superficial information, capable of producing an illusion of knowledge and distancing the subject from actual knowing <5>Postman</5><6>(Postman, 2006, [p. 74])</6>.

This form of informational circulation produces a present without historicity, in which television operates as a medium centered on the now and hinders the integration of experience into a broader temporal narrative <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 76])</2>. Public discourse thus loses the form that made it suited to rationality: under print culture, it tended toward coherence, seriousness and continuity; under televisual governance, it comes to be organized by visuality, brevity and the demand for immediate interest <3>Postman</3><4>(Postman, 2006, [p. 65-66])</4>. Information is presented in simplified, insubstantial and decontextualized form, not necessarily through explicit censorship, but because television operates as a meta-medium, directing both what is known of the world and the social ways of knowing <5>Postman</5><6>(Postman, 2006, [p. 58])</6>.

Following this change of foundation, politics, religion, news, education and commerce come to be rearranged as congenial adjuncts of <1>show business</1>, and culture tends to become a generalized arena of entertainment <2>Postman</2><3>(Postman, 2006, [p. 58-59])</3>.

The effect is not only aesthetic, but institutional, because liberal democracy depends on an informational ecology capable of sustaining discernment and deliberation. In this key, the contemporary threat to democracy need not take the form of censorship, since it is realized when political discourse takes the form of entertainment and neutralizes the very seriousness of public debate <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 91-93])</2>. By shifting the center of discourse to performance, the medium lowers the public centrality of substantive themes and weakens the social conditions of critical thought, above all when information is presented in a simplistic and non-contextual way, that is, as information packaged as entertainment <3>Postman</3><4>(Postman, 2006, [p. 92])</4>.

<1>p. 103</1> If Ellul shows technique as a structural environment, Postman makes explicit how a specific medium, television, reorganizes ways of knowing, debating and deciding. The central point is not television as an isolated historical object, but the finding that the form of the medium alters the form of socially practicable rationality. When public discourse comes to be measured by the capacity to amuse and retain attention, and not by argumentative density or the search for truth, each sphere must fit into short, emotionally marked and visually striking frames.

In this key, television inaugurates an epistemology centered on the image and on fragmented rhythm. Information arrives in brief and disconnected units, which require little effort of concentration and do not favor historical sequencing or causal reconstruction. The problem, for this thesis, lies in the formation of a cultural grammar trained to consume stimuli, and not to organize experiences into minimally stable maps of meaning.

In the digital environment, this logic does not disappear: it is intensified, personalized and made interactive. <1>Feeds</1>, <2>timelines</2>, notifications and gamified interfaces transplant to platforms the same regime of fragmentation, now combined with the permanent collection of data and the algorithmic modulation of attention. The consumer no longer merely watches the flow, since they interact with it, produce data, receive feedback and are continuously repositioned by the architecture of the service. Entertainment ceases to be<3><4>58</4></3> separate content and comes to function as a technical environment of permanence. It is in this governed flow of experiences, adjusted to maximize engagement, time spent and monetization, that the IOC comes to take shape as an object of continued enjoyment.

In transposing Postman's diagnosis to the digital environment, the decisive point is not to assert that television became the internet, but to identify structural shifts in the ecology of attention: from uniform diffusion to personalized distribution; from predominantly passive reception to continuous interaction; from crude audience metrics to the fine metrification of conduct. These shifts reorganize knowledge and attention and, therefore, have direct implications for consumption. The offer comes to depend on technical curation, while the consumer's experience becomes continuously modulable.

<1>p. 104</1> In this light, the vulnerability of the digital consumer cannot be reduced to a lack of information that more notices, terms of use or highlighted clauses could correct. The duty to inform remains relevant, but it comes to operate within an ecology in which form, curation and visibility precede reading. Before any content is actually interpreted, the technical and media presentation of the object has already defined what appears as visible, urgent, desirable or natural. The will is exercised within a repertoire of references and stimuli previously choreographed by the platform. This asymmetry in the production of meaning sets the stage for the category of semiotic vulnerability, understood as a structural disadvantage in the grammar of meanings that guides the subject's relationship with the immaterial object of consumption. Architecture thus becomes practical normativity because it organizes the field of the perceived, the credible and the natural before the informational duty can produce its effects.

Influenced by the theory of Jacques Ellul, in the work <1>Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age of </1> <2>Show Business</2> (“Divertindo-nos até a morte: o discurso público na era do show business”, our translation), originally published in 1985, the American educator Neil Postman <3>(2006)</3> investigates the influence of television on American culture, exploring the ways in which television, once it became the dominant medium of communication, transformed public discourse into entertainment and had a profound impact on the social, cultural and political epistemologies of the United States. <4>↩</4>

The cinematic acts as an editorial form of knowledge: it frames what should be seen as relevant and offers a way of reading, instead of offering technical data about items. In the official material “Still Here | Season 2024 Cinematic”, the page itself organizes the content under the title and the statement “Fight for tomorrow.” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024d)</2>. This shows the epistemological function of audiovisual content in the Postmanian sense: the content is presented as a key to interpreting the “now” and the “next”, shaping expectations and criteria of relevance, without the consumer needing to access any technical description of the object of consumption associated with the ecosystem. <3>↩</3>

The contract qualifies the object of consumption as something that is known not by inspecting the good, but through the access granted under a service regime. Riot states that it may offer the opportunity to “acquire a limited license to access [...] (‘Virtual Content’)” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. It then states that the user “has no ownership or right over any Virtual Content” and that unlocking occurs through a “limited non-transferable license” <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>. In epistemological terms, this is decisive because it shifts “knowledge of the object” outside the thing itself, since what exists legally is a permission to access. The public perception of what the item “is” comes to depend even more on the mediations that make this access intelligible and desirable. <5>↩</5>

The declared norm admits that the identity of the object may change, and this alters the type of “truth” the consumer is able to form about the item at the moment of purchase. The contract defines what is offered as “a license and a personal right [...] revocable” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. It then makes explicit the unilateral power to “delete, alter, [...] repackage, reprice” content, and records that “Virtual Products may [...] evolve over time”, including through “game balance, bug fixes, or graphic improvements” <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>. The point is not rhetorical. If the contract assumes that the item may “evolve”, audiovisual and narrative mediation comes to function as a practical source of knowledge of the good, not as ornament, because it stabilizes, on the public plane, what should be understood as the identity and value of the object, even though its configuration remains manageable and alterable. <5>↩</5>

In the religious field, Postman maintains that television converts religion, without ceremony, into entertainment, removing what made it a historical, profound and sacred practice, with the loss of ritual, dogma, tradition, theology and, above all, spiritual transcendence <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 79])</2>. In this formatting, preachers cease to be mere mediators and come to function as media protagonists, so that “their featured players become celebrities” <3>Postman</3><4>(Postman, 2006, [p. 82])</4>. The author describes this shift with explicit irony in saying that, in these programs, “the preacher is tops” and “God comes out as second banana” <5>Postman</5><6>(Postman, 2006, [p. 79])</6>. God “exists only in our minds”, while the preacher is “there, to be seen, admired, adored”, becoming the star of the show under an essentially structural logic <7>Postman</7><8>(Postman, 2006, [p. 83])</8>. <9>↩</9>

Postman's final contribution lies in a warning about the dangers of the "distracted society" that the communication mechanism had created, a concept that resonates forcefully in the contemporary context, in which the reality observed by Postman <1>(2006)</1> was raised to exponential levels through the insertion of new digital communication technologies that only reinforced and amplified the dynamics the author had observed. In this context, reflection is needed on the impacts of the media (in the broad sense) on the human capacity to think critically, to understand reality and thus to develop the skills necessary for engaged action as citizens of an increasingly complex society. <2>↩</2>
